name: Einstein's Static Field of 1912
description: Einstein's theory of static gravity from his Prague year: space stays flat and the speed of light varies from place to place, serving as the gravitational potential. Clocks slow near a mass as they do in general relativity, and light bends by half as much.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, with $c$ the speed of light where $N = 1$, so that Einstein's variable speed of light is $cN$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
The manuscript that Albert Einstein posted from Prague on 24 February 1912 had "many drops of sweat" on it, he told Wilhelm Wien, his editor [weinstein2012]. A clock deeper in a gravitational field runs slower, he had argued in 1911, and light timed by one clock for every place moves slower there too, $c = c_0(1 + \Phi/c_0^2)$ at the potential $\Phi$ [einstein1911, weinstein2012]. Now he let the speed of light be the gravitational potential itself [giulini2014prague]. A static field in this theory is a map of how fast light goes at each place, $c(x, y, z)$, laid over the flat space of Euclid, and special relativity holds wherever that speed is constant [weinstein2012, einstein1912abraham].¶What equation does $c$ obey? Einstein read it off a frame accelerating uniformly through empty space, which the equivalence principle lets pass for a uniform field [einstein1912, giulini2014prague]. There he found the speed of light growing in proportion to height, $c = c_0 + ax$, a solution of Laplace's equation, so in the presence of matter of density $ho$ he wrote $
abla^2c = kcho$, his version of Poisson's equation [einstein1912, weinstein2012]. That frame is known today as Rindler's chart of flat spacetime, and the plane where its $c$ vanishes is the horizon of the accelerated observers [rindler1966].¶On 11 March Einstein asked Wien to send the manuscript back [weinstein2012]. Not everything in it was proper, he had found [weinstein2012]. The trouble was Newton's third law: fix a set of masses to a rigid, massless frame, and by $
abla^2c = kcho$ the forces they exert on one another fail to cancel, so the frame would set itself moving [einstein1912static, giulini2014prague]. He let the paper appear and on 20 March sent a second, in which the field's own energy gravitates like any other: $
abla^2c = k\{cho + (
abla c)^2/2kc\}$, with the energy density of the gravitational field for its last term [weinstein2012, giulini2014prague]. The new equation no longer admits $c = c_0 + ax$, and the equivalence principle, he conceded, "holds only for infinitely small fields" [weinstein2012, straumann2011].¶In the second paper Einstein also gave the law of fall: a body moves so that $\int\sqrt{c^2dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2}$ is stationary [einstein1912static, straumann2011]. To a modern eye that is the geodesic equation of $ds^2 = -c(x, y, z)^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$, a spacetime whose clocks run at a rate that depends on the place and whose space is flat [straumann2011]. A conference in Prague marked the centenary in June 2012, and for it Domenico Giulini worked out the stars of the March equation [giulini2014prague]. No star of the theory fits inside a certain sphere: the equation is linear in $\sqrt{c}$, the field outside a star of mass $M$ is $\sqrt{c/c_0} = 1 - GM/2c_0^2r$, and the surface must lie outside the radius where that vanishes, a bound Giulini sets beside Hans Buchdahl's in general relativity [giulini2014prague, buchdahl1959]. Squeeze a star of given bare mass smaller and smaller, and the mass it shows the outside world goes to zero [giulini2014prague].¶How much does such a field bend light? Half of what the Sun really does: $0.83$ seconds of arc at the limb, Einstein's figure of 1911, where general relativity gives $1.7$ [einstein1911, einstein1915perihelion]. The bending has two equal sources, slowed clocks and curved space, and the field of 1912 has only the first [will2014]. Einstein carried that flat space with him to Zurich in the summer of 1912: the March equation stands on the first page of the notebook in which he hunted for the full theory with Marcel Grossmann's help, the limit every candidate had to reach [straumann2011, weinstein2012]. Field equations built on the Ricci tensor curve the space of a weak static field, which by Norbert Straumann's reading was one of his main reasons for setting them aside until November 1915 [straumann2011]. By Straumann's count the decision lost him almost three years [straumann2011].¶Max Abraham, whose own theory of gravity had taken the variable speed of light from Einstein's paper of 1911, announced that Einstein had dealt relativity "the death blow" [weinstein2012]. His answer, in July 1912, was that the constancy of the speed of light holds wherever the gravitational potential is constant, and that special relativity keeps its place as the theory of that case [einstein1912abraham, weinstein2012]. To Ludwig Hopf he described Abraham's rival theory as "a stately steed, that lacks three legs" [weinstein2012]. The flat space of 1912 went with him into the theory he published with Grossmann in 1913, and when he and Michele Besso computed Mercury's perihelion from it they got 5/12 of the advance he found in 1915 [einstein1913, weinstein2012, straumann2011]. That calculation of November 1915 showed him that space near the Sun is curved even where the field is weak, and the bending of light doubled [straumann2011, einstein1915perihelion].

related.text: The static field with no mass anywhere: at $N = 1$ the metric is Minkowski's. Einstein's uniform field is Minkowski space too, in the coordinates of uniformly accelerated observers that now carry Wolfgang Rindler's name [rindler1966].

What the field outside a body became in the finished theory. To first order in $GM/c^2r$ Schwarzschild's clocks slow as Einstein's of 1912 do, and his curved space doubles the bending of light [einstein1915perihelion].

The rival answer of the same year. Nordström kept the speed of light constant and let one factor rescale clocks and rods alike, so his light goes straight, while Einstein's field of 1912 slows the clocks alone and bends light by half of general relativity's angle [norton2007, will2014].

The weak field of a body with a number in front of every term. Einstein's bodies of 1912 sit at $\gamma = 0$, with $\beta = 1/2$ by the equation of February and $\beta = 3/4$ by that of March [will2014].

coordinates.name: Static Field

parameters.description:
Speed of light at the point $(x, y, z)$ divided by $c$, a positive pure number. Einstein's field equation of February 1912 is $
abla^2N = 4\pi Gho N/c^2$ and that of March 1912 is $N
abla^2N - 	frac{1}{2}(
abla N)^2 = 4\pi Gho N^2/c^2$, where $ho$ is the density of mass and $
abla$ the gradient of flat space

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, Cartesian on the flat space of the field. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{8\left(\partial_x\partial_y N\right)^2 + 8\left(\partial_x\partial_z N\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_x^2 N\right)^2 + 8\left(\partial_y\partial_z N\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_y^2 N\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_z^2 N\right)^2}{N^2}

coordinates.name: Uniform Field

parameters.description: Proper acceleration of a body at rest at the height $z = c^2/a$, where $N = 1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $z$ the height above the plane where $N = az/c^2$ vanishes. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outside a Body, February

parameters.description: Mass of the body as a length, $m = GM/c^2$, where $M$ is its gravitational mass; half the Schwarzschild radius of the same mass

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ centred on a static spherical body, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the distance from its centre, so that $N = 1 - m/r$ outside the body. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outside a Body, March

parameters.description: Mass of the body as a length, $m = GM/c^2$, where $M$ is its gravitational mass; half the Schwarzschild radius of the same mass

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ centred on a static spherical body, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the distance from its centre, so that $N = (1 - m/2r)^2$ outside the body. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
